provenance.other: “scorched” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Matthew 13:6 and Mark 4:6, of seed withering in the sun, and Revelation 16:9, 'and men were scorched with great heat'. Only the last has a person as its object. The adjective is from elsewhere: “burning heat” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Deuteronomy 32:24 and James 1:11, and neither uses the verb. Alma 15:3's 'he began to be scorched with a burning heat' is the Revelation construction with the other phrase's adjective. The passage's other half surfaces twelve verses later: “and they repented not” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 16:9, and “repented not of their” occurs in exactly one, Revelation 16:11, and Alma 15:15 reads 'they repented not of their sins'.
provenance.significance: Revelation 16:8-11 is one movement — the fourth and fifth vials, men scorched with great heat, and twice over the refrain that they blasphemed and repented not — and Alma 15 has split it between two men and reversed the outcome for one of them. Zeezrom is scorched, and his scorching is explicitly not a plague but a conscience: 'a burning fever, which was caused by the great tribulations of his mind, on account of his wickedness.' He repents, and is healed. Ammonihah is not scorched at all, and at 15:15 'they repented not of their sins' in Revelation's own words — and Ammonihah is destroyed by fire in the next chapter. The vial's two halves have been distributed to the man who escapes it and the city that does not.

15:3.note: 'This great sin, and his many other sins, did harrow up his mind until it did become exceeding sore, having no deliverance; therefore he began to be scorched with a burning heat.' The verb is Revelation's and the adjective is James's; the clause that completes Revelation 16:9 arrives at 15:15 in the mouth of the narrator, about the city. Held at moderate — the individual phrases are short — but the two halves of the borrowing land twelve verses apart on the two parties the chapter is contrasting, which is more than a coincidence of vocabulary.
15:3.text: And men were scorched with great heat, and blasphemed the name of God, which hath power over these plagues: and they repented not to give him glory.

provenance.other: Two KJV singletons frame the dialogue. “Believe ye that I am able” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 9:28; “according to your faith” occurs in exactly one, Matthew 9:29. Alma 15:5-10 runs the same four stages in the same order: the healers go IN UNTO THE HOUSE (Matthew 9:28, 'when he was come into the house'), the question is put — 'Believest thou in the power of Christ unto salvation?' against 'Believe ye that I am able to do this?' — the answer is the same monosyllable, 'Yea' (Matthew 9:28, 'They said unto him, Yea, Lord'), and the healing is granted on the measure of the belief: 'heal him ACCORDING TO HIS FAITH which is in Christ' against 'ACCORDING TO YOUR FAITH be it unto you.' The intervening exchange at 15:8 has a third singleton behind it: “if thou believest” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 8:37, Philip to the Ethiopian — 'If thou believest with all thine heart, thou mayest' — which is the KJV's one conditional-belief formula, and it is followed immediately by a baptism, as Alma 15:8 is followed by Zeezrom's at 15:12.
provenance.significance: Matthew 9:27-31 is the KJV's only healing conducted as a catechism. Everywhere else Jesus heals and then tells the person their faith has made them whole; here alone he asks first, receives an answer, and heals to the measure of it — which is exactly the shape of Alma 15:5-11, and it is the shape a missionary narrative needs, because a question and an answer can be preached where a miracle cannot. The Book of Mormon has also changed the object of belief in a way worth naming: Matthew's blind men are asked whether they believe Jesus is ABLE, a question about power, and Zeezrom is asked whether he believes 'in the power of Christ UNTO SALVATION' and then 'in the redemption of Christ' — the question about power has become a question about doctrine, and the healing that answers it is a conversion. Acts 8:37 supplies the second half of that conversion: the KJV's one 'if thou believest', a baptismal formula, and a baptism follows in both.

15:6.note: 'And Alma said unto him, taking him by the hand, Believest thou in the power of Christ unto salvation?' Two KJV singletons hold the two ends of this dialogue — the question at Matthew 9:28 and the measure of the healing at Matthew 9:29 — and the four stages between them run in Matthew's order, including the bare 'Yea' and the entry into the house at 15:5. A third singleton, Acts 8:37's 'If thou believest', stands behind 15:8 and is followed in both texts by a baptism. Catalogued at 15:6 as the point where the question is asked; the recurrence list carries the rest of the scene.
15:6.text: And when he was come into the house, the blind men came to him: and Jesus saith unto them, Believe ye that I am able to do this? They said unto him, Yea, Lord.

provenance.other: “took her by the hand” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Matthew 9:25, Mark 1:31 and Luke 8:54 — and two of the three are the same raising of Jairus's daughter. Mark 1:31 is the odd one out, and it is the one whose patient has a FEVER: 'Simon's wife's mother lay sick of a fever … and he came and took her by the hand, and lifted her up; and immediately the fever left her.' Alma 15:5 has Zeezrom 'upon his bed sick, being very low with a burning fever', and 15:6 has Alma 'taking him by the hand'.
provenance.significance: Of the KJV's hand-taking healings, only one is of a fever, and this chapter's patient has a fever — a fever, moreover, that the Book of Mormon has just explained psychosomatically, 'caused by the great tribulations of his mind, on account of his wickedness' (15:3). Mark 1:31 ends with the healed woman rising and ministering to the household; Alma 15:12 ends with Zeezrom baptized and beginning 'from that time forth to preach unto the people'. The pattern of immediate service after a fever is lifted is the same, and it is the only one of the three hand-takings that offers it.

15:6.note: 'Alma said unto him, taking him by the hand.' Four words shared with a three-verse phrase, and the choice among the three is made by the fever. Held at moderate: taking a sick man by the hand is what one does, and the gesture would need no source. It is written because Mark 1:31 is the single KJV verse in which that gesture cures a fever, and this is a fever.
15:6.whyNot: Four words, and the gesture is universal. Two of the three KJV verses containing the phrase are the same story, so 'exactly three' overstates the discrimination; and Acts 3:7's 'took him by the right hand', catalogued at 15:11, is a competing source for the same gesture in the same chapter.
15:6.text: And he came and took her by the hand, and lifted her up; and immediately the fever left her, and she ministered unto them.

provenance.other: “leaping up” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 3:8, and the whole clause “and he leaping up stood and walked” occurs in exactly one, the same verse. The gesture that precedes it is also absolute: “took him by the right hand” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 3:7. Alma 15:6 has 'taking him by the hand' and 15:11 has 'Zeezrom leaped upon his feet, and began to walk'.
provenance.significance: Acts 3 is the New Testament's model apostolic healing — two missionaries, a man who cannot rise, a hand taken, a leap, walking, and a crowd — and Alma 15:5-11 has all six with two missionaries of its own. What the Book of Mormon changes is the public sequel. In Acts the crowd 'ran together unto them … greatly wondering' (3:11) and Peter turns the wonder into a sermon; in Alma 15:11 the healing 'was done to the great astonishment of all the people; and the knowledge of this went forth throughout all the land of Sidom', and the sermon is preached at 15:12 by the healed man himself. Zeezrom, the lawyer who at Alma 11 was paid to trap Alma with words, is the one who begins to preach — which is the chapter's real point and is why the healing had to be public.

15:11.note: 'Zeezrom leaped upon his feet, and began to walk; and this was done to the great astonishment of all the people.' Two KJV singletons stand in the two verses of Acts 3 that this scene reproduces, and their gestures are distributed exactly as Acts distributes them: the hand at Alma 15:6 as at Acts 3:7, the leaping and walking at Alma 15:11 as at Acts 3:8, and the astonished crowd at Alma 15:11 as at Acts 3:10-11. No clause is reproduced verbatim, which is why this is an allusion; the sequence is what carries it.
15:11.text: And he leaping up stood, and walked, and entered with them into the temple, walking, and leaping, and praising God.

provenance.other: “the region round about” occurs in exactly four KJV verses: Matthew 3:5, Mark 1:28, Luke 4:14 and Luke 7:17. Three of the four are about a REPORT spreading outward from Jesus; only Matthew 3:5 is about PEOPLE coming inward, and only Matthew 3:5 is followed by a baptism — 'Then went out to him Jerusalem, and all Judaea, and all the region round about Jordan, And were baptized of him in Jordan, confessing their sins.' Alma 15:14 reads 'they did flock in from all the region round about Sidom, and were baptized.'
provenance.significance: The verse before this one has Alma establishing a church and consecrating priests 'to baptize unto the Lord whosoever were desirous to be baptized', and this one describes the response in the KJV's words for the response to John the Baptist. The place-name is put where Matthew puts Jordan — 'the region round about Sidom' for 'the region round about Jordan' — so the town takes the river's grammatical position. That is a small thing and it is the whole borrowing: what a mass baptism looks like, in the only English sentence the KJV offers for one.

15:14.note: 'For they did flock in from all the region round about Sidom, and were baptized.' One of four KJV verses, and the only one of the four that has people coming rather than a rumour going, and the only one followed by baptism. Moderate: four words, and 'the region round about' is available English — but the phrase arrives here attached to the same event it names in Matthew.
15:14.text: Then went out to him Jerusalem, and all Judaea, and all the region round about Jordan,

provenance.route: Ezekiel 3:7 with Acts 7:51 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “hardhearted” as one word occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezekiel 3:7: 'all the house of Israel are impudent and hardhearted.' Its partner is common — “stiffnecked” occurs in nine KJV verses, six of them Exodus and Deuteronomy on the golden calf, and the ninth is Acts 7:51, Stephen's 'Ye stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, ye do always resist the Holy Ghost'. Alma 15:15 pairs the singleton with the common word: 'they yet remained a hardhearted and a stiffnecked people'. The verse's last clause is Revelation's — “repented not of their” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 16:11 — and completes the borrowing begun at 15:3.
provenance.significance: Ezekiel 3:7 is not a description but a warning issued to a prophet before he is sent: the house of Israel will not hearken to you, because they will not hearken to me, because they are impudent and hardhearted. Alma has just been sent to Ammonihah, has been rejected, imprisoned and delivered, and this verse is the narrator's verdict on the mission — the one KJV word for a people constitutionally unable to hear, applied to the one city in the Book of Mormon where preaching wholly fails. Stephen's 'ye stiffnecked … ye do always resist the Holy Ghost' supplies the other half, and its charge is the one Ammonihah is about to incur in the next clause, where the power of Alma and Amulek is ascribed to the devil.

15:15.note: 'They yet remained a hardhearted and a stiffnecked people; and they repented not of their sins.' The KJV's one occurrence of 'hardhearted' is Ezekiel's word for the audience a prophet is warned about before he goes, and the pairing with 'stiffnecked' is the Book of Mormon's own. Moderate: the two words are separately available and their conjunction is not a KJV collocation.
15:15.text: But the house of Israel will not hearken unto thee; for they will not hearken unto me: for all the house of Israel are impudent and hardhearted.

provenance.other: No phrase is shared; the row is figural and is recorded as such. The KJV's charge is 'He hath Beelzebub, and by the prince of the devils casteth he out devils' (Mark 3:22, with Matthew 12:24), and the Book of Mormon's is 'ascribing all the power of Alma and Amulek to the Devil'. The relevant fact about the KJV passage is what Jesus makes of the charge: Mark 3:29-30 turns it into the one unforgivable sin, 'he that shall blaspheme against the Holy Ghost hath never forgiveness … BECAUSE THEY SAID, He hath an unclean spirit.'
provenance.significance: Alma 15:15 reports two things about Ammonihah in one sentence — that they ascribed the power to the devil, and that they 'did not believe in the repentance of their sins' — and in the KJV those two things are one thing. Mark 3:30 defines the unpardonable sin by exactly the accusation Ammonihah makes, and a sin that cannot be forgiven is a sin one cannot repent of. The city that at 14:7 asked Zeezrom 'Art thou also possessed with the Devil?' has, on the New Testament's own terms, put itself beyond the repentance it disbelieves in — and it is destroyed in the next chapter. The Book of Mormon never cites Mark 3; the sequence of the sentence does the work.

15:15.note: 'Ascribing all the power of Alma and Amulek to the Devil: for they were of the profession of Nehor, and did not believe in the repentance of their sins.' A figural link with no verbal contact, written because the two clauses of the verse stand in the same relation the KJV puts them in at Mark 3:22-30: attribute a divine power to the devil, and you have committed the sin that is not forgiven. Moderate, and the whyNot is real.
15:15.whyNot: Nothing verbal whatever is shared, and attributing a rival's miracles to the devil is a commonplace of religious polemic that needs no source. The link is an argument about the logic of the verse, not about its wording, and a reader who wants dependence demonstrated will decline it.
15:15.text: And the scribes which came down from Jerusalem said, He hath Beelzebub, and by the prince of the devils casteth he out devils.

provenance.other: “forsaken all” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 19:27 — Peter's 'Behold, we have forsaken all, and followed thee'. The synoptic parallels use the other verb: Mark 10:28 and Luke 18:28 both read 'Lo, we have LEFT all'. Two verses later Matthew itemises what forsaking all means: 'every one that hath FORSAKEN houses, or brethren, or sisters, or FATHER, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands, for my name's sake'. Alma 15:16 has Matthew's verb and Matthew's list, adapted: Amulek 'having forsaken all his gold, and his silver, and his precious things … for the word of God, he being rejected by those which were once his friends, and also by his father and his kindred'.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon has separated what Matthew fuses, and the separation is the reading. In Matthew 19:29 the possessions and the relatives are one list of things a disciple gives up. In Alma 15:16 the property is forsaken — an act of Amulek's — and the family is lost, a thing done TO him: 'he being REJECTED by those which were once his friends, and also by his father and his kindred'. Matthew's disciple leaves his father; Amulek's father leaves him. Matthew promises the forsaker 'an hundredfold, and … everlasting life'; Alma 15:18 gives Amulek the smaller and more immediate compensation, which is a house — Alma 'took him to his own house, and did administer unto him in his tribulations'. The chapter answers Peter's question, 'what shall we have therefore?', with hospitality.

15:16.note: 'Amulek having forsaken all his gold, and his silver, and his precious things … for the word of God, he being rejected by those which were once his friends, and also by his father and his kindred.' The verb is a KJV singleton and the synoptic control is clean: Mark and Luke read 'left all' where Matthew reads 'forsaken all', and the Book of Mormon has Matthew's. The itemised loss two verses later in Matthew supplies the father and the kindred.
15:16.text: And every one that hath forsaken houses, or brethren, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands, for my name’s sake, shall receive an hundredfold, and shall inherit everlasting life.

provenance.other: “strengthened his hand in God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 23:16 — 'And Jonathan Saul's son arose, and went to David into the wood, and strengthened his hand in God.' It is the KJV's only instance of one man strengthening another IN God; every other use of 'strengthened' in the Old Testament is of a king strengthening himself, or of God strengthening a man. Alma 15:18 reads 'he took Amulek and came over to the land of Zarahemla, and took him to his own house, and did administer unto him in his tribulations, and strengthened him in the Lord.'
provenance.significance: The KJV has exactly one model for what Alma does in this verse, and it is a friendship under persecution: Jonathan goes to David in the wood while Saul is hunting him, and does nothing but strengthen his hand in God. Alma 15:18 is the same act performed for a man who has just lost his property, his friends and his family for the word of God, and the Book of Mormon's phrasing shifts the preposition from Jonathan's 'in God' to 'in the Lord' while keeping the construction. It is also the last sentence of the Ammonihah narrative, and it is domestic — after burning, imprisonment, earthquake and mass baptism, the chapter ends with one man taking another home.

15:18.note: 'He took Amulek and came over to the land of Zarahemla, and took him to his own house, and did administer unto him in his tribulations, and strengthened him in the Lord.' A KJV singleton with one noun changed, and the singleton is the Bible's one scene of a friend strengthening a fugitive in God. Moderate rather than high: 'strengthened him in the Lord' is natural English and a writer could reach it without Jonathan in view, and no other element of 1 Samuel 23 is present.
15:18.whyNot: Four words, one of them altered, and the phrase is unremarkable devotional English. Nothing else of the Jonathan and David episode appears in Alma 15, and the argument rests on the rarity count plus a situational likeness.
15:18.text: And Jonathan Saul’s son arose, and went to David into the wood, and strengthened his hand in God.
